account: In a 2025 proof-of-principle study in Resuscitation, the HEART-SAFE group reported that its algorithm identified 28 of 31 circulatory arrests. The subjects were volunteers with cuff-restricted arm flow, cardioplegic surgery patients and slaughtered swine. Alerts were delivered to the HartslagNu test environment. Van den Beuken, Tuinman, Nideröst, Goossen, van Schuppen, Loer, Schwarte and Schober then reported a single case. They are of Amsterdam UMC with Utek B.V. and MiBida (the HEART-SAFE project's partners). Resuscitation Plus received the case report on 24 December 2025 and published it on 29 January 2026. Neither the report nor the journal dates the event. The authors call it the first detailed description of automated detection of a spontaneous, non-procedural cardiac arrest from consumer smartwatch data. An 82-year-old man with a right cerebellar hemorrhage and documented do-not-resuscitate directives was moved to palliative care. After about 42 hours life-sustaining treatment was withdrawn, and he died about 1.5 hours later. With the family's consent a Samsung Watch5 Pro was placed on his right wrist about 40 minutes after withdrawal. Electrocardiogram (ECG), invasive arterial pressure and clinical photoplethysmography (PPG) served as reference. The green-light PPG signal was later run through the group's previously described algorithm. It analyzes five-second windows using peak detection with minimum-amplitude safeguards. It flagged circulatory arrest when the ECG showed agonal bradycardia with the monitor reading 0/min and mean arterial pressure had fallen to 9 mmHg. Low-amplitude oscillations at about 30 per minute persisted at that point. It produced no false alarms over the observation period. The authors state that the algorithm was applied retrospectively. They say that they chose not to run it live on the device, because it is still in development and to avoid alarms disturbing the family. They state that the controlled end-of-life setting does not represent out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Samsung is not an author. The authors describe the method as peak detection; they do not describe it as machine learning. In the accompanying editorial, Veigl and Billig, who have no stake in the project, restate the authors' finding without new data. On 24 July 2026 the Radboud DETECT group reported that its own wristband algorithm detected 23 of 23 arrests in a prospective test cohort in the same end-of-life setting. That study does not test the HEART-SAFE algorithm.

ai_role.statement: The algorithm was applied after the fact to exported green-PPG data. It marked the arrest when residual pulse amplitude fell below its thresholds, shortly before the monitor flatlined, with no false alarms. It was not running on the watch and triggered nothing. Only the developers' own papers describe the event. They describe peak detection with amplitude safeguards rather than machine learning. Samsung's role is limited to the hardware.

fields.account: In a 2025 proof-of-principle study in Resuscitation, the HEART-SAFE group reported that its algorithm identified 28 of 31 circulatory arrests. The subjects were volunteers with cuff-restricted arm flow, cardioplegic surgery patients and slaughtered swine. Alerts were delivered to the HartslagNu test environment. Van den Beuken, Tuinman, Nideröst, Goossen, van Schuppen, Loer, Schwarte and Schober then reported a single case. They are of Amsterdam UMC with Utek B.V. and MiBida (the HEART-SAFE project's partners). Resuscitation Plus received the case report on 24 December 2025 and published it on 29 January 2026. Neither the report nor the journal dates the event. The authors call it the first detailed description of automated detection of a spontaneous, non-procedural cardiac arrest from consumer smartwatch data. An 82-year-old man with a right cerebellar hemorrhage and documented do-not-resuscitate directives was moved to palliative care. After about 42 hours life-sustaining treatment was withdrawn, and he died about 1.5 hours later. With the family's consent a Samsung Watch5 Pro was placed on his right wrist about 40 minutes after withdrawal. Electrocardiogram (ECG), invasive arterial pressure and clinical photoplethysmography (PPG) served as reference. The green-light PPG signal was later run through the group's previously described algorithm. It analyzes five-second windows using peak detection with minimum-amplitude safeguards. It flagged circulatory arrest when the ECG showed agonal bradycardia with the monitor reading 0/min and mean arterial pressure had fallen to 9 mmHg. Low-amplitude oscillations at about 30 per minute persisted at that point. It produced no false alarms over the observation period. The authors state that the algorithm was applied retrospectively. They say that they chose not to run it live on the device, because it is still in development and to avoid alarms disturbing the family. They state that the controlled end-of-life setting does not represent out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Samsung is not an author. The authors describe the method as peak detection; they do not describe it as machine learning. In the accompanying editorial, Veigl and Billig, who have no stake in the project, restate the authors' finding without new data. On 24 July 2026 the Radboud DETECT group reported that its own wristband algorithm detected 23 of 23 arrests in a prospective test cohort in the same end-of-life setting. That study does not test the HEART-SAFE algorithm.
